articles.title: Code Mode: the better way to use MCP
articles.why: This is the original post behind the Code Mode idea from your YouTube video. Instead of handing the model a pile of tools to call one at a time, Cloudflare turns MCP tools into a TypeScript API and lets the model write code against it in a sandbox, which cuts tokens and round trips. The follow-up posts and the REPL-style agent patterns you're seeing now all build on it.
articles.tryThis: Pick one multi-step chore you run with Claude Code (e.g. checking several job logs) and ask it to write one script that does all the steps, instead of calling tools step by step. Compare how long it takes and how much context it uses.
articles.pickReason: Starter pick — the post you mentioned tonight. Rate it to begin tuning.

articles.title: The components of agent memory
articles.why: Lance Martin lays out how Anthropic thinks about agent memory: fast capture during a session, then an offline 'dreaming' pass that checks notes against transcripts, builds linked wikis, and promotes the key notes into what loads at session start. It's the design thinking behind the memory features in tools like Claude Code, explained from the source rather than a summary.
articles.tryThis: Look at the CLAUDE.md in one Notice Conversion repo and trim it to what every session truly needs; move the rest into linked docs Claude can search, and tell it what memory is for instead of listing rigid rules.
articles.pickReason: No ratings yet, so default mix; ai-eng again from a primary source, a fresh angle after yesterday's MCP piece.

articles.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
articles.why: Coding agents write PR descriptions that are accurate but far too long for anyone to read. Willison's fix is simple: a short human-written opener up top, with the full agent text folded into a collapsible block labelled with the model that wrote it. It's a quick, practical norm for any team where agent-written PRs are starting to pile up.
articles.tryThis: On your next Claude Code PR, write two plain sentences yourself and fold the agent's write-up into a <details><summary> block. If it reads better, suggest it to your junior devs as a team convention.
articles.pickReason: Kept it short (~5 min) after the 13-min memory piece felt long; same practical, right-depth level that worked.

articles.title: The Dot and the Swarm
articles.why: Mollick argues that models now organize teams of agents on their own, so the human job shifts from designing the org chart to deciding where to aim the work and checking in as it goes. It's a clean, non-technical framing you can hand to executives who still think AI adoption means building elaborate workflows.
articles.tryThis: Next time you explain AI to a leader or small-business owner, swap 'here's the workflow to build' for 'here's the outcome to point it at and when to check its work' — and see which version lands better.
articles.pickReason: Three AI-engineering picks in a row, so leaning to the teaching mix; one of the shorter, practical leadership pieces available.

articles.title: Reasons to move to Java 25
articles.why: A compact, practical case for Java 25 as the next LTS target, written for teams still on 8, 11, 17 or 21. It walks through what actually breaks on upgrade (removed APIs, internal API use, changed GC defaults) and how to stage the move. Useful both for your own Java depth and for making the upgrade case to leadership.
articles.tryThis: Pick one batch job and run it unchanged on a Java 25 JDK in a test environment (or a homelab container); note any warnings about removed or internal APIs and GC changes, and turn that into a one-paragraph upgrade-risk note for your team.
articles.pickReason: First Java pick after a run of AI ones; kept to ~10 min since that length landed well last time.

articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
articles.why: When agents and CI became nearly all of Anthropic's git clients, merges went up more than tenfold and git mirroring stopped scaling, so they built their own server-side system in five months. It's a rare real-world account of what agent-heavy development does to CI, checkouts and code review, with numbers. The parts on reviewing the intent of agent changes and post-merge testing apply well beyond Anthropic.
articles.tryThis: Time a fresh checkout in one of your slowest GitHub Actions workflows, then try a shallow or sparse checkout (fetch-depth: 1, sparse-checkout) and compare the numbers.
articles.pickReason: Longer than your 8–10 min sweet spot, but it's fresh, primary and close to your CI work; the design-detail middle is fine to skim.

articles.title: Engineering is no longer a distraction-free job, deal with it
articles.why: Once you run coding agents in parallel, the old advice to guard long blocks of focus stops fitting the job. This short piece argues for making interruptions cheap instead, with concrete habits for keeping loops closed. It also fits a lead who gets pinged by both juniors and agents all day.
articles.tryThis: Today, before each switch away from a task, leave one finished 'pebble' (a draft PR, a sent reply, a one-line note of the next step) instead of an open loop, and turn agent/chat sounds into silent badges.
articles.pickReason: Focus topic hadn't come up yet, and after a 17-min pick yesterday this is a quick ~5-min read.

articles.title: Claude's new auto eval tool
articles.why: Hamel, one of the most trusted voices on LLM evals, puts Anthropic's new Claude Code eval commands through a real trial. It's a quick, honest look at where the agent helps and where you still have to look at the data yourself.
articles.tryThis: Next time Claude Code proposes a test or eval for you, open the actual prompt or assertion it wrote and check it against a few real outputs before trusting its summary.
articles.pickReason: Short Claude Code piece from a source that values practical takeaways, kept brief since a few picks are still unread.

articles.title: What 1,000 small business owners taught us about AI
articles.why: A field report from Anthropic's in-person workshop tour for small-business owners, mostly trades and logistics firms. It lays out what actually moved people: security questions first, a guided hands-on build, and hearing peers' solutions. It's a ready-made blueprint for how you'd run your own sessions.
articles.tryThis: Sketch a 90-minute workshop outline using its pattern: 15 min on data/privacy, 45 min guided build of one real reporting workflow, 30 min of attendees sharing problems — then test it on one local owner or a coworker.
articles.pickReason: ai-teach hadn't come up since Nov 20, which you finished and tagged work/teach; kept it ~8 min.
